beats.text: YouTube now lets creators group Shorts into *seasons* and episodes.
Most brand Shorts end on a logo. Nothing pulls anyone to *episode two.*
Cut every episode one beat early. End on the *question*, not the answer.
Write five lines. One per episode. *Then* book the shoot.

social.ig_caption:
One Short is an ad. Five is a show.

YouTube now lets creators group Shorts into seasons and episodes that play in order.

Most brand Shorts end on a logo or a discount code. There's nothing to come back for.

Try this before your next shoot: write the season in one line, then one line per episode. Each one ends on a question.

Comment STORY and we'll send you the five-line season planner.

Full post on the blog (link in bio).
social.linkedin_post:
YouTube just made it easier to turn Shorts into a show.

Shorts series let creators group Shorts into seasons and episodes, with sequential playback. It's rolling out to channels in the YouTube Partner Program.

The feature matters less than what it says about the audience. YouTube's own post on microdramas says 40% of their views came more than 30 days after a video went live. A good episode keeps working. A one-off ad usually doesn't.

Most D2C brand Shorts are built like tiny ads. Hook, product, logo, discount. Every new one starts from zero.

So here's the brief I'd write instead. One line for the whole season. One line per episode. Each episode ends on an open question.

A habit from the edit suite: cut each episode one beat early. Stop on the question, before the answer. Finished feels good in the edit. For a series, finished is the enemy.

If your channel doesn't qualify for the feature yet, publish in numbered episodes anyway. Build the habit before you have the button.

Story first. Camera second. Spend third.

Full breakdown on the Payoff blog.
